title: The preacher's senses (Kern ch. 18)
hookLine: those who keep the sutra have their senses purified

lines: MUSIC OFF, ROOM FULL OF SOUND.
cards: Turn off the music, close the laptop, and the room turns out to be full of sound: the fridge's hum, a car two streets over, a bird, a pipe ticking, your own breath. None of it is new.
It was there the whole time, underneath. Chapter eighteen of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, is about senses made clear like that.
It promises the one who keeps this teaching eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body and mind that take in the world without fog.

teach.b: First, who the preacher is. The Sanskrit is dharmabhanaka, one who speaks the dharma.

In the Lotus it isn't only a monk on a platform: it's any son or daughter of good family who keeps this teaching, reads it, recites it, explains it or copies it out. A parent reading at bedtime would count.

Second, the eyes. With the very eyes their parents gave them, the Buddha says, such a person will see the whole universe, from the lowest hell to the highest heaven, and the beings in it, and how their deeds bear fruit.
Not new eyes, not a third eye.

The chapter's list of what they will hear goes on and on: elephants and horses, chariots, weeping and laughter, conches, bells and drums, the voices of men, women, boys and girls, the sounds of gods and of beings in pain.
And the ear takes all of it in without being overwhelmed. Fourth, body and mind.

The chapter goes on through smell, taste and touch, and says the body becomes so clear that beings see themselves reflected in it, like a mirror. The mind, hearing even a single verse, finds many meanings opening from it.
One way to hear all this: purified senses are not superpowers. They are senses that receive the world as it is, before the story about it takes over.

how: In schools that center the Lotus Sutra, keeping the sutra means reading, reciting, explaining and copying it, practices open to lay people as well as monks and nuns; this chapter describes the purified senses said to follow.

o: everyday senses made clear by keeping the teaching
a third eye that opens after years of meditation
magic powers granted only to the greatest monks

games.q: the preacher's senses: tap the pairs.
p: the same ones their parents gave
clear as a mirror for beings

s: the 'preacher' in this chapter means only an ordained monk
the chapter speaks of any son or daughter of good family who keeps, reads, explains or copies the sutra.
the sutra says the purified eyes are the same eyes given by one's parents
not new eyes; the same ones, made clear.
the clear ear in this chapter is overwhelmed by all it hears
the text says it takes in every sound without being overwhelmed.

games.q: you keep this teaching, and your ears become clear. the world arrives all at once: elephants, bells, weeping, laughter. what happens?
o: you have to shut some of it out
you hear all of it, and none drowns the rest
you hear only the pleasant sounds
games.why: the chapter says the cleared ear takes in every sound, pleasant and painful, without being overwhelmed.

practice: With eyes closed or resting low, open the ears: find the farthest sound, then the nearest, then everything in between, letting each arrive and leave without naming it.
If a sound is unpleasant, notice the urge to push it away, and hear it anyway, simply as sound. If you lose the thread, the next sound will bring you back.

wordCard.voice: The preacher's senses. In the Lotus Sutra, the eyes, ears and mind of one who keeps the teaching, made clear enough to take in the world without being overwhelmed. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one who speaks the dharma; the Lotus Sutra's word for anyone who keeps and teaches it.

carryVoice: Your line: clear senses. The same eyes and ears your parents gave you, only clearer. See you tomorrow.
